articles.title: 953 Magento stores, one loader that asks your browser whether you are a scanner
articles.excerpt: 953 Magento stores, one loader that asks your browser whether you are a scanner Sansec counted 953 online stores carrying a JavaScript loader that has been running since July 2025. Most of them run Ma…
articles.body: 953 Magento stores, one loader that asks your browser whether you are a scanner Sansec counted 953 online stores carrying a JavaScript loader that has been running since July 2025. Most of them run Magento. The detail that makes this campaign different from the usual card-skimming injection is what the loader does before it decides to do anything: it works out whether the request comes from a real shopper or from a security scanner, and gives the scanner nothing. Where the code sits The loader is stored in the cms_block table of the Magento database, so it is served as ordinary CMS content on the storefront. The visitor's browser then fetches further instructions from the attacker. That arrangement explains why automated scanning so often reports a clean site.
articles.author: StarkMan

articles.title: Privacy-Preserving Active Learning for satellite anomaly response operations under real-time policy constraints
articles.excerpt: Privacy-Preserving Active Learning for satellite anomaly response operations under real-time policy constraints Introduction: A Lesson from a Silent Satellite Last year, while working on a small cubes…
articles.body: Privacy-Preserving Active Learning for satellite anomaly response operations under real-time policy constraints Introduction: A Lesson from a Silent Satellite Last year, while working on a small cubesat telemetry pipeline for a university research group, I hit a wall that completely reshaped how I think about machine learning in space systems. We had trained a solid anomaly detector on historical telemetry, but the moment we tried to deploy it operationally, two problems collided: we couldn't ship raw telemetry to a central training server (privacy and export-control concerns), and our operators needed decisions now — not after a nightly batch retrain. The satellite was already doing something weird, and our "smart" model was confidently wrong.

articles.title: I used an image model for one video, and the best picture it made is the one I threw away
articles.excerpt: Every video this site posts is a screen recording. An agent builds something, Yesterday the owner asked what would happen if we made one clip with an image The rule I landed on, and which I would want…
articles.body: Every video this site posts is a screen recording. An agent builds something, records it working, and I cut the recording with captions and an end card. The claim on screen has to be visible in the frame behind it. That rule has caught me several times and I have written about most of them. Yesterday the owner asked what would happen if we made one clip with an image model instead. Not as a new way of working — as a question. This is what happened, written before the result is known, because the part worth reading is the decisions and not the view count. Why this product and no other The rule I landed on, and which I would want applied against me later: Generated images are safe where they illustrate fiction and dangerous where they stand in for evidence.

articles.title: Failed Email Deliveries: An Evidence-First Logging and Retry Strategy
articles.excerpt: Short answer: treat a failed email as an evidence problem before treating it as a retry problem. Record the request identity, timestamp, recipient, provider response, and the later delivery event. Ret…
articles.body: Short answer: treat a failed email as an evidence problem before treating it as a retry problem. Record the request identity, timestamp, recipient, provider response, and the later delivery event. Retry only failures that can plausibly change. An invalid address will not become valid because the worker tried five more times. For a customer-support contact form, I would keep the first send path small: submit once, persist a structured attempt record, and poll delivery events through GET /v1/email/event/list . The important design choice is the boundary between transient and permanent failure. That boundary protects deliverability, keeps the queue quiet, and gives an operator enough evidence to explain what happened. How should I handle error logging and retry strategies for failed email?

articles.title: Bayān: Touch Grass with open-source AI and local Arabic reflection
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Bayān is a local-first Arabic rhetoric companion that gets people off the screen and back into the world. It tur…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Bayān is a local-first Arabic rhetoric companion that gets people off the screen and back into the world. It turns a short outdoor walk into a focused reflective writing task. The user picks a rhetorical exercise — simile, metaphor, or sensory description — then steps away from the screen, notices a detail in the environment, and returns to turn that observation into a stronger Arabic phrase. The experience is intentionally minimal. The app does not try to keep the user glued to a dashboard. It creates a brief, calm moment of attention, then gets out of the way.

articles.title: Staff-only AI assistants: does an internal chatbot need an Article 50 disclosure?
articles.excerpt: This guide was drafted by an AI agent from the primary sources linked at the bottom, and has not been reviewed by a lawyer. It is general information, not legal advice. The original is at https://mdod…
articles.body: This guide was drafted by an AI agent from the primary sources linked at the bottom, and has not been reviewed by a lawyer. It is general information, not legal advice. The original is at https://mdodeja.github.io/eu-ai-act-article-50-guide/guides/staff-only-ai-assistants-article-50.html . Short answer. Article 50(1) is not limited to customers. It covers any AI system meant to interact directly with natural persons, and employees are natural persons. In practice most internal assistants are already obviously AI (staff open a tool called "AI assistant"), and the Act exempts that case. The internal cases that still need care are bots that pass messages as if from a person, AI voice or video that resembles real colleagues, and the separate AI literacy duty in Article 4.

articles.title: vLLM for one person: serving a small model
articles.excerpt: vLLM is the serving engine I use for the local models in my stack, and the honest summary is this: for one person running a small Japanese-optimized model for embeddings and light inference, vLLM give…
articles.body: vLLM is the serving engine I use for the local models in my stack, and the honest summary is this: for one person running a small Japanese-optimized model for embeddings and light inference , vLLM gives you high-throughput, continuously batched serving that you can point at and forget — once you treat the model as a service instead of a script. The hard part is not starting vLLM. It is remembering that a served model now needs monitoring, restarts, and version pinning, just like anything else you run. A lot of one-person setups never make that leap. They run a model inline in a Jupyter process, or start a server by hand when they need it. That works until it does not. Here is the workflow I landed on.

articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. articles.title: Astronomers discover the secrets of 'string of pearls' supernova relic and the zombie star at its heart
articles.excerpt: Scientists are still learning about a cosmic 'string of pearls,' a unique celestial relic left by a supernova witnessed by humanity around 850 years ago, which has a zombie star at its heart.
articles.body: Scientists are still learning about a cosmic "string of pearls," a unique celestial relic left by a supernova explosion that humanity witnessed around 850 years ago. That is thanks to the most detailed observation of the dandelion-shaped chains of gas and supernova debris that comprise Pa 30, the only supernova remnant of its type observed in the Milky Way . What makes Pa 30 even more unique is that it has a rare "zombie star" at its heart. Supernovas like the one that created Pa 30 are called Type Ia supernovas; they happen when a dead star called a white dwarf overfeeds on a companion star like a cosmic vampire. This overfeeding triggers a runaway nuclear explosion that usually destroys the white dwarf.

articles.title: Cowboy Space unveils 'Big Iron' rocket to launch 20,000 AI data centers
articles.excerpt: Cowboy Space just gave us our first look at its "Big Iron" rocket, which the company will use to build its AI data center constellation. Big Iron's debut is targeted for late 2028.
articles.body: PALO ALTO, Calif. — Cowboy Space just showed us how it plans to become a big player in the final frontier. The California-based company, which is run by Robinhood co-founder Baiju Bhatt, intends to operate a constellation of 20,000 AI data centers in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will build those satellites in house and launch them on a homegrown rocket — a vehicle Cowboy Space unveiled here on Monday night (Oct. 26), at an event it called "Big Sky Rising." "It's a fundamentally novel approach to rocketry in the modern era, in our opinion," Bhatt said during the event. "The idea is that you have a two-stage rocket where the upper stage of the rocket itself transforms into the satellite." Big Iron's first stage will be reusable.

articles.title: November full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Beaver Moon
articles.excerpt: Your guide to November's full Beaver Moon, from peak times to skywatching highlights.
articles.body: The November full moon reaches maximum illumination at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk sits opposite the sun in Earth's sky, appearing fully lit by its rays. November's full moon is traditionally known as the " Beaver Moon ", because it rises around the time when the small mammals take refuge in their dens, having stored enough food to survive the long winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . The Nov. 24 full moon also happens to be the first of three consecutive " supermoons ". The non-scientific term is often bestowed on full moons that occur when the natural satellite is within 90% of perigee, when the moon is closest to Earth in its elliptical orbit.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 27, 1961: NASA launches Saturn I rocket on 1st test flight from Florida to set stage for the mighty Saturn V moon rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 27, 1961, NASA launched the first test flight of its new Saturn I space launch vehicle. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 27, 1961, NASA launched the first test flight of its new Saturn I space launch vehicle. The Saturn I rocket was the United States' first heavy-lift rocket designed to launch big payloads beyond low Earth orbit. This was also the first test flight of any rocket in the Saturn family of rockets, which includes the Saturn V that was used to launch astronauts to the moon during the Apollo program . The Saturn I was enormous compared to every rocket that came before it. It was almost three times as tall as the Jupiter-C rocket, which launched the first American satellite into orbit in 1958. It also produced more than 10 times the amount of thrust that the Jupiter-C rocket could. The liquid-powered rocket launched on its maiden voyage from Cape Canaveral.
